title: Router Session Grid
eyebrow: Design for approval · changes the open-session screen, nothing built yet

short.lead: What exists now: one session open at a time on the right, with three buttons, the whole conversation and a terminal panel under it. This design turns the right side into a grid of tiles you arrange however you like. Each tile is one session, showing its last few messages and a Resume button until you resume it, then its terminal filling the tile. Tiles move and resize with the mouse or to an exact percentage you type, and they can spread across your monitors. The project list becomes a tile too, so it can move, shrink or go to another screen.
short.hint: Tap an item to see what it changes and what it needs from you.
items: Sessions as tiles in a grid

Clicking a session in the list, or dragging it into the grid, opens it as a tile. A tile's header moves it beside, above or below another tile, and dropping it onto another tile stacks the two as tabs. Pulling the edge between tiles resizes them, and the neighbours adjust to fit. Putting four terminals for four projects side by side takes a few drags.

items.alt: Mock-up: the project list as a tile on the left, and four session tiles in a 2x2 grid. Three show Claude Code running; one shows its last messages and a Resume button. A blue divider shows 50% while being dragged.
items.caption: One monitor with the list tile and a 2x2 grid of sessions.

items: A preview, then one Resume button

A tile that isn't running shows the last three messages and when it was last active, with one large Resume button. Resume runs Claude Code in the tile, and the terminal takes the whole tile. A small icon in the tile's header opens it in Windows Terminal instead, out of the way.
Open another grid window on any monitor and drag tiles between windows. Each window remembers its monitor, its tiles and their sizes.
Choose how a second monitor works: answer the first question, 'How should a second monitor work?', in Your choices.

Every tile's header shows which account it runs on, by its email address, next to its limits, and the top bar shows the account a new session would use. Claude Code records the signed-in email in .claude.json in each Claude folder, which is where the router reads it. A menu on the account name switches that tile to another account.
Choose how switching works: answer the third question, 'How should switching accounts work?', in Your choices.

Besides dragging, a tile's menu lets you type its width or height as a percentage of the window. Quick layouts (1, 2 side by side, 2x2, 3 and 1) arrange the open tiles in one click, and you can save your own layout by name.
After you approve, I'll write a build plan and create the issues, then build it.
Pick your answer to each question in Your choices, then tap Copy my reply and send it.

changes: new
Grid layout
Tiles you move, resize and stack.

Built on dockview, a free, open-source library (MIT licence) that already handles dragging, resizing, tabs, floating tiles and pop-out windows, so no other libraries are needed. I rendered a 2x2 grid with it inside Chromium, the browser engine the app uses, and it showed no errors. Each tile header keeps the session's three small bars: context, 5-hour limit and weekly limit.
Fixed list on the left and one session on the right.
A grid where every tile, including the list, can be moved and sized.
You set the screen up the way you work.
new
Monitors
More than one window, one per monitor.
Every window has the same grid and can hold the list tile, project tiles or session tiles. Closing the app saves every window's monitor, position and tiles, and opening it puts them back.
One window.
A window per monitor, with tiles dragged between them.
Your second screen can hold its own sessions.

changes: keep
What stays
Finding sessions, the list's search and folding, the usage limits, and Claude Code running in the terminal.

The project list, search, folding, clean titles, the limits strip, account choice for new sessions and the quit prompt all stay. The website keeps today's read-only view, because a website can't start programs or open windows on other monitors.
choices: screens
How should a second monitor work?
A
A full grid window per monitor
Open a new window, put it on any monitor, and arrange tiles in it like the main one. Drag tiles between windows.
B
Pop single tiles out into their own windows
Any tile can float in its own small window that you place anywhere. Simpler, but each window holds one tile, so a second screen of four sessions is four windows.
C
Stretch one window across all monitors
One big grid. Tiles can straddle the gap between screens, and Windows' own snapping and full-screen work poorly with it.
Option A gives every monitor the same freedom as the main window. It also covers what option B offers, because a window in option A can hold just one tile.
projects
How should projects sit in the grid?
A
The list is a tile, and any project can be dragged out as its own tile
A project tile lists just that project's sessions, so a monitor can show, say, PlunderSpell's sessions on their own.
B
The list is a tile, and only sessions go in the grid
Simpler: one list, and the grid holds only session tiles.
Option A matches what you asked for: projects get the same movable, resizable layout as sessions.
account
How should switching accounts work?
A
Each account gets its own Claude folder, and any tile can switch

The router sets up a folder for each of your three accounts once, and you sign in to each one once. After that, switching a tile's account continues the same conversation on the other account: the router copies the conversation file across, so nothing is lost, and resumes it there. Each tile can be on a different account at the same time.
B
Keep one folder and switch by signing in again
A Switch account button runs Claude Code's /login for you. Every session on that folder moves to the new account at once, and you can't have two accounts running side by side.

Option A is what makes routing work: one session can move to the account with room while others keep going. Your screenshots show one Claude folder today, so this adds a one-time sign-in for each of the other two accounts.
restore
When you open the app again, what should the tiles do?
A
Come back in place, each showing its preview and Resume button
Nothing runs until you press Resume, so no usage limit is spent by surprise.
B
Come back in place and resume Claude Code in every tile
Fastest to get going, but every tile starts Claude Code at once.
Option A never spends usage without you asking, which matters when a 5-hour limit is at 99%, as in your screenshot.

wrapup.summary: Replace the single open session with a grid of movable, resizable tiles across as many monitors as you like, each tile a short preview with a Resume button and then its terminal.
